docs.title: 2. 🔁 The Update Loop: Opt-In Cloud Review, Proposals & Approval
docs.text:
Nothing is uploaded and nothing changes in the running WAF unless you say so, twice.

  1. Local enforcement (free, always local). Requests are normalized and evaluated against the compiled clauses on your node. Novel anomalies are recorded in waf_ledger.db as patterns awaiting analysis; recording them uploads nothing.
  2. Opt-in upload. Set auto_sync_enabled = true to let a background timer send the recorded minterms to SATGuardian cloud synthesis every autonomous_sync_interval_secs seconds, or trigger one batch yourself: 
    ./satguardian-waf sync-simplify --limit 100
# or, on the admin listener:
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SATGUARDIAN_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  http://127.0.0.1:10001/api/waf/sync-simplify
  3. Results land as proposals. A cloud review run stores what comes back with dynamic_clauses.applied = 0. Proposals do not enter the running engine, are not loaded at boot, and change nothing until you approve them.
  4. You decide. Review each proposal and approve or discard it: 
    ./satguardian-waf clauses list
./satguardian-waf clauses apply <clause_id>
./satguardian-waf clauses reject <clause_id>
    Or over the admin API (GET /api/waf/clauses/pending, POST /api/waf/clauses/{id}/apply, DELETE /api/waf/clauses/{id}), all behind the admin token.
  5. Approval is what makes a clause live. Approving registers the clause in the running engine's in-memory dynamic-clause table, so new requests are evaluated against it immediately with no restart and no dropped TCP connections. If the proxy is stopped, approved clauses are the only proposals loaded at startup; pending ones stay pending. A clause that duplicates a mask already active, or exceeds the engine's dynamic-clause cap, is saved but will report that it enforces on restart instead of now. The hot list is a RwLock-protected clause table in src/engine/sat_solver.rs; there is no lock-free ArcSwap swap in this code base.
  6. Rejecting discards a proposal only. It never deletes a rule that is already enforcing; enforced clauses are not touched by the reject path.

The same shape applies to the advisor: satguardian-advisor.py analyses the ledger and proposes; applying anything is a separate, explicit operator action.

docs.title: 3. 🛠️ Customization & Business Rules Guide
docs.text: SATGuardian allows fine-grained customization through two primary mechanisms: Declarative Business Rules and Digital Twin Verification.

docs.title: 3.1 Declarative Business Access Rules in waf_config.toml
docs.text:
Define granular access policies per path prefix, HTTP method, client IP whitelist/blacklist, and mandatory headers under [business_rules]:

[business_rules]
enabled = true

# Example Rule 1: Strict API Method Restrictions
[[business_rules.rules]]
id = "biz-api-methods"
name = "Strict API Method Whitelist"
path_prefix = "/api/v1/"
allowed_methods = ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"]
blocked_methods = ["TRACE", "CONNECT", "PATCH"]
allowed_ips = []
blocked_ips = []
required_headers = []
max_body_bytes = 10485760 # 10 MB payload ceiling
enabled = true

# Example Rule 2: IP-Whitelisted Administrative Gateway
[[business_rules.rules]]
id = "biz-admin-gateway"
name = "Admin Portal IP Restricted Access"
path_prefix = "/internal/admin/"
allowed_methods = ["GET", "POST"]
blocked_methods = []
allowed_ips = ["127.0.0.1", "10.0.0.1", "192.168.1.100"]
blocked_ips = []
required_headers = ["X-Admin-Token"]
max_body_bytes = 1048576 # 1 MB
enabled = true

docs.title: 3.2 Digital Twin Rule Verification
docs.text: Before you approve a rule, satguardian-advisor.py can replay it against recorded history (a Digital Twin replay): 1. Reads the benign HTTP transactions recorded in waf_ledger.db. 2. Evaluates candidate rules against that historical traffic and reports any collisions. Replay quality depends on the ledger contents; there is no fixed FPR floor. 3. Only after you approve does a clause reach active memory: it is registered in the engine's in-memory clause table and starts evaluating new requests, with no restart and no dropped TCP connections. Traffic is never hot-reloaded from the cloud by itself.

docs.title: 4. 🧰 Suite Applications & Tooling Guide
docs.text: The repository ships one native Rust binary plus a set of Python CLI utilities for analysis, administration, monitoring and benchmarking.

docs.title: 1. Main Engine Binary: satguardian-waf (Rust Engine & CLI)
docs.text: Subcommands as implemented (satguardian-waf --help is authoritative). --config is a global flag accepted by every subcommand.

docs.title: A. Standalone Reverse Proxy Mode
docs.text:
# Launch the proxy using a configuration file
./satguardian-waf proxy --config waf_config.toml

# Or override the listener and upstream on the command line
./satguardian-waf proxy --listen 0.0.0.0:8080 --upstream http://127.0.0.1:3000

# Mode and response verbosity
./satguardian-waf proxy --mode monitor --verbose
proxy also serves the management API on admin_listen_addr (127.0.0.1:10001 by default, 503 until SATGUARDIAN_ADMIN_TOKEN is set) and starts the background cloud review timer only if auto_sync_enabled = true.

docs.title: B. Native Benchmark Mode
docs.text:
Measures in-memory evaluation latency and CPU throughput over N synthetic requests (default 10,000). It exercises the engine only: no TLS, no proxy hop, no upstream. 

./satguardian-waf benchmark --requests 10000
Reference point: the pinned in-memory run over corpus/independent_v1.json at 10,000 requests measured about ~0.46 ms p50 and ~0.9–1.0 ms mean, with p99 ~6 ms (re-measured 2026-11-10). In-memory figures only — quote them as such.

docs.title: C. Standalone Inspection Mode (CLI Payload Test)
docs.text:
Inspects a single request and prints its 128-bit FeatureVector (u128) and the decision trace: 

./satguardian-waf inspect --method POST --path /api/search \
  --query "id=1' UNION SELECT * FROM users--"

docs.title: D. Cloud Review, One Batch at a Time
docs.text:
Sends the pending anomaly minterms to SATGuardian cloud synthesis and stores the result as proposals. The running rule set is not changed by this command. 

./satguardian-waf sync-simplify --limit 100

docs.title: E. Approve or Discard Proposals
docs.text:
./satguardian-waf clauses list            # what is waiting for a decision
./satguardian-waf clauses apply <id>      # make it enforce
./satguardian-waf clauses reject <id>     # discard the proposal (never removes an active rule)

docs.title: F. Envoy ext_authz Service and SafeLine T1K Co-Processor
docs.text:
./satguardian-waf envoy-authz --listen 0.0.0.0:9002
./satguardian-waf envoy-authz --socket /var/run/waf.sock

./satguardian-waf t1k-server --listen 0.0.0.0:8000   # SafeLine T1K protocol

docs.title: G. Cloud Account Status
docs.text:
Checks the SU balance and the edge entitlement reported by the cloud: 

./satguardian-waf entitlement

There is no separate api subcommand: the management API runs inside proxy on the loopback admin listener described in §1.3.

docs.title: 2. Forensic Advisor & Digital Twin: satguardian-advisor.py
docs.text: Analyses recorded transactions in waf_ledger.db, clusters novel patterns (patterns awaiting analysis), replays candidate rules against the ledger, and produces evidence-backed audit reports. It analyses and proposes — applying anything stays an explicit operator action.

docs.title: Usage:
docs.text:
# Evidence-backed audit report in interactive HTML format
python satguardian-advisor.py --report audit_report.html

# Same report in Markdown
python satguardian-advisor.py --report-md audit_report.md

# Custom SQLite ledger path
python satguardian-advisor.py --db /path/to/custom_ledger.db --report custom_report.html

# Analyse and list suggestions without prompting to apply anything
python satguardian-advisor.py --dry-run

docs.title: 3. Business Rules & Islands Manager: satguardian-rules.py
docs.text: Interactive manager for [business_rules] and [islands]: list, add, toggle and delete customer rules, flip islands, run a live inspection through the management API, and drive the advisor. It writes changes into waf_config.toml as well.

docs.title: Usage:
docs.text:
python satguardian-rules.py            # curses TUI (Linux/macOS, or windows-curses)
python satguardian-rules.py --cli      # ANSI console menu when curses is unavailable

Two limits worth knowing: * The tool has no subcommands — satguardian-rules.py list does not exist; the menu is interactive. * It calls the management API but does not send the admin token, and its default --api value is http://127.0.0.1:10000 while the WAF binds 127.0.0.1:10001. Point it at the admin listener with --api http://127.0.0.1:10001; API-backed actions only work once the management API is enabled with SATGUARDIAN_ADMIN_TOKEN, and the tool has no way to pass that token, so editing waf_config.toml through the tool (option 8) is the path that works against a token-protected listener.

docs.title: 4. Real-Time Terminal Dashboard: satguardian-top.py
docs.text:
htop-style terminal monitor that reads waf_ledger.db directly: throughput (req/sec), recorded evaluation latencies (µs), and the blocked-attack distribution by category and source IP. It is local and read-only — it opens no socket and uploads nothing.

The latencies shown are the in-memory evaluation times recorded per request by the engine; they exclude TLS, proxy hops and upstream time.

docs.title: Usage:
docs.text:
python satguardian-top.py                     # auto-discovers the ledger
python satguardian-top.py --db /var/lib/satguardian/waf_ledger.db --rate 0.5 --blocks-only

docs.title: 5. Interactive Web Dashboard: run_web.py
docs.text: Serves the PoC dashboard and duel simulator from satguardian_waf/web with FastAPI/uvicorn (not Streamlit, and there is no app.py): visual telemetry over the Python reference engine, attack trend charting and rule inspection.

docs.title: Usage:
docs.text:
python run_web.py 8002
Open http://localhost:8002. The dashboard exercises the Python reference implementation, not the Rust engine.

docs.title: 6. Multi-WAF Comparative Benchmark Suite: run_benchmark.py
docs.text: Runs the Python reference harness against local Python stand-ins for CRS-style, semantic-token, raw-regex and probabilistic techniques. It does not execute Coraza, SafeLine, ModSecurity or a trained NLP model. The dataset is the small in-repo payload list, and the report prints provenance and a disclaimer.

docs.title: Usage:
docs.text:
# Run comparative benchmark across 1,000 requests
python run_benchmark.py 1000

docs.title: 7. Rule-Set Health Report: satguardian-health.py
docs.text: Local, read-only audit of the rule set you wrote: inventory of business rules and islands (enabled vs disabled), structural findings (duplicate ids, a rule that both allows and blocks the same method, duplicate bodies, contradicting overlapping path prefixes) and a summary of what the ledger recorded. It reads waf_config.toml and waf_ledger.db, opens no socket and uploads nothing — it is part of the free tier and works with no cloud account.

docs.title: Usage:
docs.text:
python satguardian-health.py                       # text report from the current directory
python satguardian-health.py --json                 # machine-readable
python satguardian-health.py --config /etc/satguardian/waf_config.toml --db /var/lib/satguardian/waf_ledger.db
python satguardian-health.py --strict --top 10      # exit 1 if any WARN finding is present

A line-by-line review of the satguardian repository and adjacent workspace projects (hesize-code-ia, adn, guardian-api-, optimizador_bayesiano, f32) distinguishes implemented code from external research concepts:

Technical Concept Status in satguardian Actual Code Implementation & Location Multi-Pass Lexical Normalization & Tokenization ✅ Implemented src/ast/lexer.rs (AstLexer) and satguardian_waf/core/solver_sat.py unwind nested URL/HTML encodings, strip /*...*/ comments, and extract structural tokens across 5 attack domains (SQLi, XSS, RCE, LFI, SSRF). 128-Bit Feature Vector (u128) ✅ Implemented src/ast/features.rs (FeatureVector { bits: u128 }, 40 named variables in the current catalogue) packs HTTP metadata, Shannon entropy flags, and lexical token presence into a 128-bit integer. Bitmask Conjunction Evaluator ("SAT Engine") ✅ Implemented src/engine/sat_solver.rs (SatguardianSatEngine) evaluates pre-compiled boolean cubes per rule via bitwise AND: (fv.bits & required_mask) == expected_bits. (Note: It is a fast bitmask evaluator, not an in-path backtracking DPLL/CDCL SAT solver). Opt-in Cloud Review Client ✅ Implemented src/cloud/satguardian_client.rs (SatguardianCloudClient::simplify, compile_equation_to_clauses()) posts the pending minterms to the SATGuardian cloud synthesis service at https://satguardian.tech/api/simplify and compiles the answer into bitmask clauses. auto_sync_enabled defaults to false (src/config.rs, waf_config.toml), so no upload happens until the operator turns it on. It is server-side, is not distributed to customers, and this audit could not review its code; the client only receives and evaluates the compiled clauses. Proposal Gate for Cloud Clauses ✅ Implemented src/ledger/sqlite_ledger.rs stores cloud clauses with applied = 0 (propose_dynamic_clause); startup loads approved rows only (load_applied_clauses, applied = 1). Decisions are explicit operator actions behind the admin token: satguardian-waf clauses list / apply / reject, GET /api/waf/clauses/pending, POST /api/waf/clauses/{id}/apply, DELETE /api/waf/clauses/{id}. Rejecting deletes only a proposal; a rule already enforcing is never removed by it. Approved Clause Goes Live Without a Restart ✅ Implemented SatguardianSatEngine::register_dynamic_clause appends to the in-memory clause set the proxy shares through Arc; an HTTP approval is visible to subsequent requests with no process restart and no dropped connections. The earlier description of this step as automatic hot-reload of whatever the cloud returned is no longer true. Digital Twin Benign Traffic Replay ✅ Implemented satguardian-advisor.py (SimulationAgent) replays candidate rules against benign requests recorded in waf_ledger.db and reports collisions. It does not certify a fixed false-positive rate. Stateful Burst Rate Limiting ✅ Implemented src/stateful/limiter.rs (StatefulRateLimiter, per-client records behind an RwLock<HashMap<..>>) and src/stateful/sliding_window.rs (SlidingWindowRingCounter) count requests per client IP over a sliding window and raise the SAT-STATE-01 violation that src/engine/sat_solver.rs turns into a block. (There is no DashMap token bucket in this codebase; an earlier revision of this table claimed one.) docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
Modern Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) face a fundamental engineering tension between inspection latency, evasion resistance, and false positive rates. Unnormalized regular expression engines are cheap per request but miss nested encodings and inline comments. Anomaly-scoring rule sets transform several request targets and evaluate many rules. Token-weight classifiers can fire on benign technical prose. Those statements are design-level; this repository does not benchmark the real products, only local Python stand-ins.

This paper presents the implemented architecture and the measurements available for SATGuardian Edge WAF (satguardian). SATGuardian decouples in-path request evaluation from out-of-band rule review, and puts an operator decision between the two: 1. In-Path Hot Plane (Native Rust): Applies bounded multi-pass lexical normalization (src/ast/lexer.rs), packs structural tokens and request attributes into a 128-bit integer (FeatureVector { bits: u128 } in src/ast/features.rs), and evaluates compiled rule cubes via bitwise operations ((fv.bits & required_mask) == expected_bits in src/engine/sat_solver.rs). On the pinned corpus at 10,000 requests, a representative run measured p50 ~0.46 ms, mean ~0.94 ms, and p99 ~6 ms, single-threaded, in memory only (re-measured 2026-11-10; an earlier run on a smaller rule set reported ~20 µs). 2. Out-of-Band Review Plane (Rust & Python, opt-in): Logs anomalous u128 minterms to a local SQLite ledger (waf_ledger.db). Only if the operator turns cloud review on (auto_sync_enabled, false by default) are those minterms sent to SATGuardian cloud synthesis at satguardian.tech, which minimizes them over the {AND, OR, NOT, XOR} basis server-side. The client compiles the returned equation into bitmask clauses and stores them as proposals (dynamic_clauses.applied = 0). Nothing is enforced until the operator approves a proposal; approved clauses then register in the running engine without a restart.

docs.title: 1.1 Lexical Normalization & Feature Vector Mapping
docs.text:
Let an incoming HTTP request be represented by the tuple \(r = (M, P, Q, H, B)\) denoting method, path, query string, headers, and body.

The lexical normalizer \(\mathcal{N}\) (src/ast/lexer.rs) applies bounded iterative percent-decoding (\(k \le 3\) passes) and inline comment stripping (/*...*/) to produce a canonical byte stream \(s = \mathcal{N}(r)\), from which it extracts a set of structural tokens \(\mathcal{T}(s)\) and maps \(r\) into a 128-bit boolean feature vector:

\[\mathbf{v}(r) \in \{0, 1\}^{128} \quad (\text{represented in Rust as } \texttt{u128})\]

Each bit \(v_i \in \{0, 1\}\) (\(i \in \{0, \dots, 127\}\)) encodes a deterministic predicate (e.g., presence of SQL tautology tokens, UNION SELECT projection, executable <script> or inline DOM event attributes, shell command chaining operators, relative path traversal sequences, or high character Shannon entropy \(H(s) > \tau\)). The u128 container addresses up to 128 variables; the catalogue in src/ast/features.rs names 40 of them today, and that catalogue is exactly what the client sends to the cloud service.

docs.title: 1.2 In-Path Bitmask Cube Evaluation (src/engine/sat_solver.rs)
docs.text:
Each compiled security rule \(c_j\) is a boolean cube (product term / conjunction of literals) represented by two 128-bit integers: - required_mask (\(M_j \in \texttt{u128}\)): Bitmask indicating which positions of the vector participate in rule \(j\). - expected_bits (\(E_j \in \texttt{u128}\)): Expected polarity (1 for positive literal, 0 for negated literal) of those active variables.

At runtime, evaluating whether request \(\mathbf{v}(r)\) triggers rule \(c_j\) requires a single bitwise AND and equality check:

\[\text{Match}(\mathbf{v}(r), c_j) \iff (\mathbf{v}(r) \mathbin{\&} M_j) == E_j\]

If no rule cube matches (\(\forall j, \, (\mathbf{v}(r) \mathbin{\&} M_j) \neq E_j\)), the security invariant holds and the request is allowed. Unlike backtracking regular expressions or NP-complete in-path DPLL/CDCL solvers, bitwise evaluation over \(R\) rules executes in deterministic \(O(R)\) CPU cycles.

docs.title: 1.3 Out-of-Band Cloud Synthesis and the Approval Gate (src/cloud/satguardian_client.rs, src/ledger/sqlite_ledger.rs, src/api/server.rs)
docs.text:
When previously unobserved minterms \(\mathcal{M} = \{m_1, m_2, \dots, m_k\} \subset \{0, 1\}^{n}\) (\(n \le 128\)) accumulate in waf_ledger.db, the client can ask the service to reduce them:

  1. Request. SatguardianCloudClient::simplify posts the variable catalogue and the pending minterms to https://satguardian.tech/api/simplify. This only happens if the operator opted in: auto_sync_enabled is false by default in src/config.rs and waf_config.toml.
  2. Minimization, server-side. Reducing \(\mathcal{M}\) to a compact formula \(c^*\) over \(\{\land, \lor, \neg, \oplus\}\) is done by SATGuardian cloud synthesis. That minimizer is not part of this repository, is not distributed to customers, and its internal algorithm and reduction behaviour are not characterized by any measurement here.
  3. Compilation, client-side. compile_equation_to_clauses() parses the returned equation into runtime pairs \((M_j, E_j)\), i.e. (required_mask, expected_bits), so the hot path stays a single AND plus one comparison per clause. An equation that does not parse is refused (invalid_cloud_equation) and the ledger is left unchanged.
  4. Proposal, not enforcement. Each clause is stored with applied = 0 (SqliteLedger::propose_dynamic_clause). The running engine does not see it and startup skips it — load_applied_clauses() selects applied = 1 only. The HTTP response says so: "status": "proposed".
  5. Digital-twin replay as evidence. satguardian-advisor.py (SimulationAgent) replays candidate bitmasks against the benign records in waf_ledger.db and reports collisions per run, so the operator decides with the replay in front of them. On the bundled demo ledger the current run prints, for example, 154 collisions for the hostile-IP candidate and No collisions / 1663 allowed for the method-restriction candidates. The ledger is demo data, so neither outcome establishes a false-positive rate.
  6. Approval. satguardian-waf clauses apply <id> or POST /api/waf/clauses/{id}/apply (admin token) registers one clause in the engine; the HTTP call applies it to the live process, the CLI applies it from the next start. reject deletes only a proposal and never removes a rule already enforcing.

docs.title: 2. Evaluation: What Was Measured, and What Was Not
docs.text: One real-product comparison exists. Section 2.5 reports a 2026-11-09 head-to-head against Aegis Community Edition v1.1.0 (Coraza engine, bundled OWASP CRS 4.25.1, paranoia level 1) over real HTTP. All other competitor rows in this repository are local Python stand-ins — not Coraza, SafeLine, ModSecurity or any commercial product — and their numbers describe this repository's stand-ins only.

docs.title: 2.1 Detection: In-Sample Floors and the One Held-Out Measurement
docs.text:
corpus/independent_v1.json holds 63 labelled attacks and 16 benign controls; corpus/heldout_v1.json holds 17 attack variants and 4 benign controls. Both were used to drive fixes after their first run, so their current scores are regression floors. corpus/heldout_v2.json (98 attacks, 57 controls) was labelled first and run once, before any fix. The current out-of-sample measurement is benchmarks/real_comparative/corpus/heldout_v10.jsonl (70 attacks, 44 controls), also run once before any fix on 2026-11-08; the heldout_v2 figure (56.1%/7.0%) remains for provenance.

Corpus First run (before fixes) Current regression run Interpretation independent_v1 51/63 attacks (80.95%), 3/16 benign blocked (18.75%) 63/63 attacks, 0/16 benign blocked In-sample regression floor after fixes heldout_v1 11/17 attacks (64.71%), 0/4 benign blocked (0.00%) 17/17 attacks, 0/4 benign blocked Batch consumed by the fix pass; in-sample regression floor heldout_v2 55/98 attacks (56.1% recall, 95% CI 46.3–65.5%), 4/57 controls blocked (7.0% FPR, 95% CI 2.8–16.7%) not re-run; tuning against it would invalidate the batch Held-out, one run on 2026-11-04; superseded as the headline estimate heldout_v10 current engine: 70/70 attacks (100% recall), 0/44 controls blocked (0.0% FPR); frozen one-shot: 27/70 detected, 0/44 blocked one-shot frozen in corpus/heldout_v10_report.json; current behaviour in corpus/heldout_v10_post_tuning_report.json Held-out batch measured once on 2026-11-08 before tuning — the publishable blind estimate is the frozen one-shot result; 100%/0.0% is the current-engine diagnostic

The heldout_v10 row is the number to quote today: on a harder batch — protocol bodies, query DSLs and admin surfaces the earlier corpora never covered — the engine caught 27 of 70 attacks with zero false positives. The earlier v2 figure (56.1%/7.0%) stays published for provenance; batches v3–v9 were each measured once and spent as tuning inputs, and heldout_v2_report.json / heldout_v10_report.json carry the per-category breakdowns and every individual miss. The current 100%/0% regression rows mean only that the pinned cases still pass; they are not held-out estimates and they are not evidence of accuracy on real traffic. There is no third-party or independent evaluation: every batch, including heldout_v10, was written inside this project from public payload catalogues and labelled by the same side that owns the engine, and its benign controls are imagined traffic, not a sample from a real access log. Rules for adding cases and the full miss list live in corpus/README.md.

docs.title: 2.2 In-Memory Latency (Native Rust)
docs.text: satguardian-waf benchmark -r 10000 cycles the corpus and measures rule evaluation only. A representative run on the development machine reported p50 near 0.46 ms, mean near 0.94 ms and p99 near 6 ms, single-threaded (re-measured 2026-11-10). The figures move with machine load and should be re-measured on the target host. Excluded from the measurement: network, TLS, reverse-proxy hops, upstream calls, and SQLite ledger writes. The runner prints these exclusions and the in-sample caveat on every run, and it refuses to start if the corpus file is missing.

docs.title: 2.3 Python Reference Harness (Local Stand-Ins)
docs.text:
python run_benchmark.py 1000 runs the Python reference port of the engine against the local stand-ins on the in-repo payload list. Every row is labelled with its provenance in the report output, the Markdown export and the API response. Representative 1,000-request values:

Engine Implementation Attacks detected Benign blocked Mean latency SATGuardian Python reference Python port (not the Rust engine) 100.0% 0.0% ~0.06 ms CRS-style anomaly stand-in Python reimplementation 97.3% 0.0% ~0.24 ms Semantic-ruleset stand-in Python reimplementation 94.4% 0.0% ~0.06 ms Token-weight stand-in Python heuristic 77.3% 24.6% ~0.07 ms Unnormalized regex stand-in Python reimplementation 76.5% 0.0% ~0.04 ms

Both the payload list and the stand-ins were written in this repository, so these are in-sample results over a small hand-written set. They show that the harness runs end to end. They do not support any claim about real products, and they do not establish production readiness.

docs.title: 2.4 Engineering Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Normalization drives the detection gap. The first-run misses were concentrated in MySQL executable comments, || tautologies, HTML-entity schemes, overlong UTF-8, \u-escaped keys and nested Log4Shell lookups. The fixes were lexical: additional decoding passes and normalization rules, not a larger rule table.
  2. Structural conjunctions avoid keyword false positives in the pinned set. The three first-run false positives were a <script src> include, a data: URI and a localhost URL in prose. Requiring co-occurring structural tokens removed them without deleting the cases.
  3. Per-request cost is dominated by normalization, not rule matching. The bitmask test is one AND plus one comparison per rule; the decode loop runs first and sets the floor. This ordering is why the in-memory figure is tens of microseconds rather than single digits.
  4. One held-out run is not an independent evaluation. heldout_v10.jsonl is a real out-of-sample measurement of those payloads — the frozen one-shot recorded its frozen one-shot result and 0.0% false-positive rate (95% CI 0.0–8.0%), while the current engine measures 100%/0.0% on the same batch as a post-tuning diagnostic. The earlier batches (including heldout_v2 at 56.1%/7.0%) are regression floors. A defensible quality claim still needs batches built and labelled by people outside this project, repeated held-out runs, and a long-running soak under real traffic. None of that exists, and no third-party evaluation has been run. See STATUS.md.

docs.title: 2.5 First Head-to-Head Against a Real WAF Product (Aegis Community v1.1.0)
docs.text:
On 2026-11-09 the engine was replayed against Aegis Community Edition v1.1.0, a shipping WAF built on the Coraza engine with the bundled OWASP CRS 4.25.1 LTS ruleset at paranoia level 1 in blocking mode, over real HTTP on localhost using the same corpus files. This is the first measurement in this repository against an actual product rather than a local stand-in. Run manifest and per-case verdicts: benchmarks/real_comparative/results/aegis/ (RUN.json, aegis_v10.jsonl, aegis_crs.jsonl).

Corpus SATGuardian Aegis + CRS 4.25.1 PL1 crs_v430.jsonl (4,050 vendor-authored attacks) 82.0% recall (3,321) 80.7% recall (3,268) heldout_v10.jsonl (70 attacks) 100% post-tuning diagnostic; frozen one-shot 68.6% recall (48/70) heldout_v10.jsonl (44 controls) 0.0% FPR post-tuning diagnostic; frozen one-shot 0.0% 36.4% FPR (16/44) benign_heldout_v3_v10.jsonl (665 pooled benign controls) 0.5% FPR (3/665; v10-only non-spent subset 0/44) 22.9% FPR (152/665)

Union of both engines on crs_v430 reaches 92.9% recall; their intersection is only 69.8%. The engines miss different rule families (e.g. SATGuardian 44/44 vs Aegis 7/44 on CRS rule 934140; Aegis 210/330 vs SATGuardian 162/330 on rule 944300), so a cascade or ensemble is the natural deployment shape — a product story a CRS-only vendor cannot copy. On benign traffic the gap is sharper still: pooled over 665 benign controls, Aegis blocked 152 (22.9% FPR) versus SATGuardian's 3 (0.5%; only the 44 v10 controls are non-spent for SATGuardian).

Limits of the run: Aegis executed CRS 4.25.1 (the corpus targets 4.30), paranoia level 1 only, community edition, plain HTTP, localhost, dummy upstream, and its default rate limiter was disabled for isolation. latency_us is not comparable across engines (full HTTP round-trip vs in-process evaluation). One run, one configuration — not a product ranking.

docs.title: 3. Self-Hosted Deployment & the Security Units (SU) Review Model
docs.text:
The whole model in one sentence: free, you get local protection on your own node; paying, you get continuous review of new patterns, update proposals and explanations — without ever giving up control of your WAF.

  • No traffic hosting: your DNS CNAMEs never point at SATGuardian servers. The Edge WAF runs where you put it — as a standalone Rust binary, a reverse proxy in front of Nginx/Apache/IIS, or an Envoy sidecar in Kubernetes talking ext_authz over a Unix Domain Socket (/var/run/satguardian/waf.sock).
  • Edge inspection carries no per-request fee: the in-path plane is free and unlimited, needs no network access to enforce, and keeps working if the cloud is unreachable or the plan lapses.
  • What a paid plan buys is review, not control of your WAF: the SATGuardian cloud synthesis service analyses the patterns your node recorded and returns update proposals with their equation, reduction and replay evidence. That service is metered in Security Units (SU) against the variables and minterms it compresses; when a plan's monthly SU quota is exhausted it returns HTTP 402 SU_QUOTA_EXHAUSTED, cloud review pauses, and the node keeps enforcing the clauses you already approved. The current plan table lives in the project README and on the product site; this paper does not restate prices, and no plan comes with an SLA or a coverage guarantee.
  • Control is the product feature: cloud results land in your ledger as proposals (dynamic_clauses.applied = 0), never in the engine. Only satguardian-waf clauses apply <id> or an admin-token POST /api/waf/clauses/{id}/apply makes one enforce; reject discards a proposal and cannot remove a rule already in force; and auto_sync_enabled stays false until you turn it on.

docs.title: 4. Positioning: Why Deploy SATGuardian
docs.text:
SATGuardian is not "another WAF". It is a deterministic decision layer that does what signature- and scoring-based firewalls structurally cannot:

  1. Every decision is auditable, bit by bit. A block is a Boolean cube (feature_vector & mask) == expected over a 128-bit feature vector — reproducible and reviewable by an auditor without trusting a vendor's scoring internals. CRS-style engines report an anomaly score; SATGuardian reports which structural tokens, in which combination, triggered which rule.
  2. It complements existing WAFs instead of replacing them. In the 2026-11-09 head-to-head against Aegis Community v1.1.0 (§2.5), the two engines reached parity on the CRS v4.30 suite (82.0% vs 80.7% recall) with strongly complementary coverage: union 92.9%, intersection 69.8%. As a cascade stage it adds detections signatures miss; alone, it adds explainability they cannot offer.
  3. Traffic sovereignty is architectural, not contractual. No DNS redirection, no hosted gateway, no per-request fee; the only optional cloud contact is opt-in review of recorded feature vectors, returned as proposals an operator approves.
  4. Free edge, paid governance. Edge inspection is free and unlimited; the paid layer is review — pattern analysis, update proposals and explanations metered in Security Units.

Who this is for: teams that must prove why a request was blocked — regulated workloads, audit-driven security programs, and operators who want a fast deterministic first stage in front of a heavier WAF. Who it is not for (yet): teams needing a managed console, TLS termination, geo-blocking or rate limiting in the same box — those belong in the proxy/TLS layer in front of SATGuardian.
